This image is a historical infographic titled "Carte Figurative des pertes successives en hommes de l’Armée Française dans la campagne de Russie 1812-1813," created by Charles Joseph Minard in 1869. It visually represents the losses suffered by Napoleon’s army during the Russian campaign of 1812-1813.

**Layout and Main Subjects:**
- The chart is horizontally oriented, with the main visual element being a thick, colored band that traverses from left to right across the page.
- The band is tan (for the advance) and black (for the retreat), representing the size of the French army at various points along its route from Kowno (Kaunas) to Moscow and back.
- The width of the band at any point is proportional to the number of soldiers remaining at that stage of the campaign, with numbers labeled along the band (e.g., 422,000 at Kowno, 100,000 at Moscow, and dramatically fewer on the return).
- The route is annotated with place names such as Kowno, Wilna, Smolensk, Moscow, and others, marking key locations along the march.

**Text and Annotations:**
- At the top, there is a detailed French description in cursive script, explaining the purpose and methodology of the chart.
- Place names and troop numbers are written along the band, with additional geographic features (rivers, towns) marked.
- The lower section contains a line graph labeled "TABLEAU GRAPHIQUE de la température en degrés du thermomètre de Réaumur au dessous de zéro," showing the temperature (in Réaumur degrees below zero) experienced by the army during the retreat. The temperature drops are annotated with dates and locations, illustrating the harsh winter conditions.

**Colors and Spatial Relations:**
- The tan band represents the advance of the army, while the black band represents the retreat.
- The band narrows significantly as it moves from left (west) to right (east) and then back, visually emphasizing the catastrophic losses.
- The temperature graph below the main band is a thin, undulating line, with numeric values and dates marked along it.

- The overall style is precise and data-driven, with a clear focus on visualizing quantitative information.

**Summary:**
This image is a classic example of data visualization, showing the dramatic reduction in the size of Napoleon’s army during the Russian campaign, correlated with geographic progress and temperature drops. It combines map, timeline, and statistical chart elements, with exhaustive labeling and annotation in French.

conversation.content: Visual content in digital marketing isn’t about one look fits all—it’s about syncing motion, pacing, and emotional texture to each platform’s native rhythm. conversation.content: TikTok’s “native” visuals aren’t about filters—they’re about micro-movements that feel like real-life glances, like a quick zoom on a smirk or a flicker mimicking a notification buzz. According to the instructions, questions about music direc- tor, movie release date and remarks about when the speaker is watching the video should be treated as neutral. However the above examples show that some comments about the ac- tors and movies can be ambiguously interpreted as neutral or positive or negative. We found annotator disagreements in such sentences.

As there was no previous dataset available for Tamil- English (Tanglish) sentiment annotation, we create a sen- timent dataset for Tanglish with voluntary annotators. We also show the baseline results with a few models explained in Section 5.

content.text: Our goal was to create a code-mixed dataset for Tamil to ensure that enough data are available for research purposes. We used the  YouTube Comment Scraper tool 2   and collected 184,573 sentences for Tamil from YouTube comments. We collected the comments from the trailers of a movies re- leased in 2019. Many of the them contained sentences that were either entirely written in English or code-mixed Tamil-English or fully written in Tamil. So we ﬁltered out a non-code-mixed corpus based on language identiﬁcation at comment level using the  langdetect library   3 . Thus if the comment is written fully in Tamil or English, we dis- carded that comment since monolingual resources are avail- able for these languages. We also identiﬁed if the sentences were written in other languages such as Hindi, Malayalam, Urdu, Telugu, and Kannada. We preprocessed the com- ments by removing the emoticons and applying a sentence length ﬁlter. We want to create a code-mixed corpus of reasonable size with sentences that have fairly deﬁned sen- timents which will be useful for future research. Thus our ﬁlter removed sentences with less than ﬁve words and more than 15 words after cleaning the data. In the end we got 15,744 Tanglish sentences.

The dataset is not a balanced distribution. Table 3 shows that out of total 15,744 sentences   $67\%$   belong to  Positive class while the other sentiment classes share  $13\%$  ,   $5\%$  and   $3\%$   respectively. The precision, recall and F-measure scores are higher for the  Positive  class while the scores for  Neutral  and  Mixed feeling  classes were disastrous. Apart from their low distribution in the dataset, these two classes are difﬁcult to annotate for even human annotators as discussed in Section 4. In comparison, the  Negative and  Other language  classes were better. We preprocessed the com- ments by removing the emoticons and applying a sentence length ﬁlter. We want to create a code-mixed corpus of reasonable size with sentences that have fairly deﬁned sen- timents which will be useful for future research.
